content.text: An aggregate isn't "the root plus everything related to it". Evans defines it as a boundary for consistency and transactions: what's inside must satisfy its rules every time a change commits. Vaughn Vernon's advice follows from that: design small aggregates, reference other aggregates by identity, and keep them in step with eventual consistency. A big object graph costs you load time and false conflicts, and buys no extra correctness.
Checkout gets slower every month. Placing an order loads the
Customer

aggregate: profile, addresses and every order the customer ever placed, with their lines. For a loyal customer that's thousands of objects in memory to add one order. Then the second complaint arrives: when support updates a customer's phone number while she's checking out, one of the two saves fails with a version conflict. Nothing about a phone number affects an order, yet both changes go through the same root, so they collide.
The common misconception

The belief: an aggregate is a root entity with everything related to it hanging underneath, so the whole object graph can be loaded, navigated and saved together. A customer has orders, so orders go inside the customer.
It's a reasonable reading of the definitions. Fowler describes an
aggregate
as "a cluster of domain objects that can be treated as a single unit", and says "you request to load or save whole aggregates." ORMs make navigation properties easy, and
customer.Orders

reads naturally. Vernon's essay opens with exactly this question, "Is an aggregate just a way to cluster a graph of closely related objects under a common parent?", and its fictional team falls into the trap by putting weight on the words "Products have".

The half-truth: an aggregate is a cluster with one root, loaded and saved as a whole. But what decides membership is which rules must hold together in one transaction, not which objects happen to be related.
What actually happens
Aggregates exist to protect invariants

Evans's DDD Reference starts the pattern from a problem: "It is difficult to guarantee the consistency of changes to objects in a model with complex associations." The answer is to cluster objects, choose a root, allow outside references to the root only, and "Define properties and invariants for the aggregate as a whole". Then: "Use the same aggregate boundaries to govern transactions and distribution." Fowler is just as direct: "Transactions should not cross aggregate boundaries." Vernon sums it up: "aggregate is synonymous with transactional consistency boundary", and aggregates "are chiefly about consistency boundaries and not driven by a desire to design object graphs."
Big aggregates fail in two ways
The first is contention. In Vernon's example, Bill plans a backlog item and Joe schedules a release on the same product. The aggregates use
optimistic concurrency

, so Joe's save fails: the product's version changed under him. Vernon's verdict: "Nothing about planning a new backlog item should logically interfere with scheduling a new release!" The big cluster was built on "false invariants", constraints the developers invented rather than real business rules. Evans warns that cautious locking makes users "interfere pointlessly with each other", and Microsoft's Azure guide says combining aggregates forces "unrelated updates to compete for the same locks."
The second is load. Vernon describes "thousands of backlog items" loaded into memory "just to add one new element to the already large collection". Collections that start empty grow for years.
Small, by identity, eventually consistent

Vernon's rules, which Microsoft's guide repeats: design small aggregates, containing "only the data that must remain consistent within a single transaction"; reference other aggregates by identity, the way a delivery stores a drone's ID instead of the drone; and use
eventual consistency
outside the boundary. Evans says the same: "Within an aggregate boundary, apply consistency rules synchronously. Across boundaries, handle updates asynchronously." A
domain event
raised by one aggregate is the usual way to update another later.

Small can mean very small. Microsoft notes that an aggregate can be a single entity: "What makes it an aggregate is the transactional boundary." Vernon reports one project where about 70% of aggregates were just a root entity with value-typed properties, while stressing that this ratio won't hold for every domain.
The fix: one aggregate per consistency rule

tabs.label: ❌ Wrong
✅ Right

content.text: Placing an order now creates one
Order

and saves it, without loading the customer at all. A phone change and a checkout touch different aggregates, so they no longer collide. Rules that span both, such as awarding loyalty points, react to an order-placed event in their own transaction. Screens that need a customer with their order history get it from a query, not by loading aggregates, and Vernon suggests CQRS when those queries get expensive.

rows.text: An aggregate holds everything related to its root
It holds what must be consistent within one transaction
They cause false conflicts and load thousands of objects to change one
Aggregates should reference each other as objects
Reference other aggregates by identity, like a delivery storing a drone's ID
One request should update all related data atomically
Evans: synchronous inside a boundary, asynchronous across boundaries
It can be a single entity; the transactional boundary is what makes it one

blocks.title: A reference doesn't extend the boundary

content.text: Holding a reference to another aggregate, or a navigation property in EF Core, makes it tempting to change both in one save. Vernon is explicit that a reference "does not place the referenced aggregate inside the consistency boundary of the one referencing it." Changing several aggregates in one transaction is often a sign that a boundary is wrong.

Vernon credits Eric Evans with a simple tie-breaker: if keeping the data consistent is the job of the user running the use case, make it transactionally consistent. If it's another user's job, or the system's, let it be eventually consistent. Vernon adds that domain experts are sometimes far more comfortable with delays than developers are.

Vernon allows that "An experienced DDD practitioner may at times decide to persist changes to multiple aggregate instances in a single transaction, but only with good reason", such as a screen that creates a batch of items at once. Treat it as a documented exception, not the default.
How to apply it in your project
For your largest aggregate, write down the rules that must hold every time a change commits. Ask domain experts which ones are real and which a developer invented.

items.title: Draw a boundary around each rule's data

content.text: Keep together only the data one rule needs to check. Everything else becomes its own aggregate, often a single entity.
Store
CustomerId
, not
Customer
. Let the application service load what a command needs, and serve screens from queries instead of aggregate graphs.
When one change must trigger another, raise a domain event and handle it in a separate transaction, and agree with the business how long the delay may be.
Key takeaways

items.text: An aggregate is a transactional consistency boundary, not a container for everything related.
Only data that must be consistent at commit time belongs inside; many aggregates are a single entity.
Big aggregates cause false conflicts between unrelated edits and load far more than each change needs.
Reference other aggregates by identity, and keep them in step with domain events and eventual consistency.
Ask whose job consistency is: the current user's job means one transaction, anyone else's can wait.
